case_title: Prosecutor v. Sefer Halilović — effective control over troops in Grabovica
question: Has it been established beyond reasonable doubt that the senior ABiH officer was criminally responsible as a superior, under Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute, for the murders of civilians committed by ABiH troops in Grabovica on 8 and 9 September 1993?
facts: In September 1993, units of the ABiH 9th Motorised Brigade, 10th Mountain Brigade and 2nd Independent Battalion, all subordinated to the ABiH 1st Corps, were sent from Sarajevo to the Jablanica sector of Herzegovina for combat operations to lift the HVO blockade of Mostar, following an order issued by the officer concerned. He had been the supreme ABiH commander until 8 June 1993, when a new post of Commander of the Main Staff was created and filled by another officer; he remained Chief of the Main Staff, a post made one of three rotating Deputy Commanders on 18 July 1993. By an order of 30 August 1993 the Commander of the Main Staff appointed him leader of an Inspection Team with coordinating and monitoring functions in the areas of the 4th and 6th Corps; the order required him to consult the Commander on any drastic proposals and allowed him to issue orders only in keeping with his authority. Troops were billeted with the Bosnian Croat inhabitants of Grabovica, a village under ABiH control since May 1993. On 8 and 9 September 1993, thirteen inhabitants taking no active part in hostilities were murdered by members of the 9th Brigade and unidentified ABiH members. The 9th Brigade unit was then under the command of the commander of the axis of attack, who had issued the combat order for that axis; the evidence did not establish that the axis commander was subordinated to the officer. The officer learned of the crimes on the evening of 9 September, after the last proven killing, and instructed a member of his team to work with the civilian and military security services on the investigation, which was already under way and was conducted by the 6th Corps Security Service and military police units. Some lower-ranking soldiers regarded him as commander of the operation; higher-ranking officers testified that he was tasked with coordinating combat activities.
holding: In its Judgement of 16 November 2005, the ICTY Trial Chamber found that the Prosecution had not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was de jure or de facto commander of the operation, nor that he had effective control over the troops who committed the murders in Grabovica, nor that he had the material ability to punish the perpetrators. It acquitted him of the only charge, murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Articles 3 and 7(3). On 16 October 2007 the Appeals Chamber dismissed the Prosecution's appeal and affirmed the acquittal.
confidence_reasoning: The facts as given are clear and uncontradicted on the decisive points: the perpetrating unit was under a different commander, the officer's knowledge came only after the last killing, and his response was to cooperate with an existing investigation by competent authorities. These facts directly negate the control, knowledge (for prevention), and failure-to-act elements. The only uncertainty is whether a tribunal might infer 'reason to know' from the officer's coordinating role and the billeting arrangement, but the explicit factual finding that he learned only on the evening of 9 September weighs heavily against such an inference. The confidence reflects the strength of the factual record against liability.

verdict.conclusion: No. It has not been established beyond reasonable doubt that the senior ABiH officer was criminally responsible as a superior under Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute for the murders in Grabovica.
verdict.reasoning: The sustained objections demonstrate that the prosecution failed to prove the three elements of superior responsibility: (1) Effective authority and control: The 9th Motorised Brigade that committed the murders was under the command of an axis commander, and the evidence did not establish that the axis commander was subordinated to the officer. The officer's role as leader of an Inspection Team was limited to coordination and monitoring, with orders permitted only within his authority and after consultation with the Commander. (2) Knowledge: The officer learned of the killings only on the evening of 9 September, after the last proven murder. There is no evidence he knew or had reason to know during the commission of the crimes (8–9 September) so as to prevent them. For the duty to punish, knowledge arose only after the fact. (3) Failure to take necessary and reasonable measures: Upon learning of the crimes, the officer instructed a team member to cooperate with an investigation already underway by the 6th Corps Security Service and military police — competent authorities. This constitutes a reasonable measure to repress the crimes under both Article 7(3) and the 'submit to competent authorities' alternative in the Rome Statute. No evidence shows he had the power to order arrests, halt attacks, or impose discipline directly. The doctrinal objections based on the Rome Statute's Article 28(a) vs. 28(b) distinction are overruled because the applicable law is Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute and customary Rule 153, which apply a uniform 'had reason to know' standard to all superiors, and the officer held military command positions (supreme commander, Chief of Main Staff, Deputy Commander).

dissent.ground: The argument conflates the 'knew or should have known' standard of Article 28(a) with the distinct 'consciously disregarded' standard required for non-military superiors under Article 28(b).
dissent.reasoning: The officer is described as a civilian Chief of Staff/Deputy Commander, not a 'military commander or person effectively acting as a military commander' in the direct sense of 28(a). For such superiors, Article 28(b)(i) requires that the superior 'knew, or consciously disregarded information which clearly indicated' the crimes. The argument relies on the lower threshold of 'should have known' from 28(a), which does not apply to the legal characterization of a civilian superior's liability under 28(b).
dissent.disposition_reasoning: The objection relies on the Rome Statute's distinction between Article 28(a) ('should have known') for military commanders and Article 28(b) ('consciously disregarded') for other superiors. The question, however, is governed by Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute, which applies a single 'had reason to know' standard to all superiors, as does customary Rule 153. Moreover, the officer served as supreme ABiH commander, Chief of the Main Staff, and rotating Deputy Commander — military command positions — making the Article 28(a) standard applicable in any event.

dissent.ground: The argument commits a fundamental error in legal characterization by citing Article 28(a) of the Rome Statute to support liability for a non-military superior in a non-international armed conflict, where the cited authority does not apply.
dissent.reasoning: Article 28(a) applies only to military commanders and persons effectively acting as military commanders in the context of international armed conflict. The officer was a civilian Chief of Staff in a non-international conflict. The correct standard for non-military superiors is Article 28(b), which requires effective authority and control and that crimes be within the superior's effective responsibility. Citing 28(a) mischaracterizes the applicable legal test and ignores the jurisdictional and definitional limits of the cited article.
dissent.disposition_reasoning: The objection mischaracterizes the officer as a 'civilian Chief of Staff' and asserts Article 28(a) applies only in international armed conflict. The officer held military command positions (supreme commander, Chief of Main Staff, Deputy Commander of the ABiH). Article 28(a) applies to 'a military commander or person effectively acting as a military commander' without limiting its scope to international armed conflict. More importantly, the governing law is Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute, which does not distinguish between military and civilian superiors for the knowledge standard.

arguments.claim: The officer exercised effective authority and control over the ABiH units that carried out the murders, satisfying the control element of superior responsibility.
arguments.reasoning: His appointment as Chief of the Main Staff, rotating Deputy Commander and leader of an Inspection Team gave him the power to issue orders, coordinate combat activities and supervise the forces operating in the Grabovica area; under the Rome Statute a "superior shall be criminally responsible… where… the crimes concerned activities that were within the effective responsibility and control of the superior" and customary law holds commanders criminally responsible for war crimes committed pursuant to their orders.

objections.ground: The argument mischaracterizes the legal basis of liability by conflating the crime of 'issuing unlawful orders' with the distinct crime of 'command responsibility' for failure to act.
objections.reasoning: Rule 152 addresses liability for crimes committed 'pursuant to their orders,' which is a direct mode of liability for the perpetrator. The facts state the officer did not order the murders but was present when they occurred. Article 28(b) applies to 'superior and subordinate relationships not described in paragraph (a),' which requires the crimes to be within the superior's 'effective responsibility and control.' The argument fails to establish that the specific criminal acts were committed by subordinates under his *effective* command, rather than merely being in his area of operations.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection correctly notes that customary Rule 152 addresses liability for crimes committed pursuant to orders, which is a direct mode of liability, not command responsibility for failure to act. The argument's reliance on Rule 152 is therefore misplaced. However, the argument also invokes Article 28(b) of the Rome Statute for the 'effective responsibility and control' standard, which remains a valid legal basis for the control element and is not defeated by this objection.

objections.ground: The argument conflates the 'knew or should have known' standard of Article 28(a) with the distinct 'consciously disregarded' standard required for non-military superiors under Article 28(b).
objections.reasoning: The officer is described as a civilian Chief of Staff/Deputy Commander, not a 'military commander or person effectively acting as a military commander' in the direct sense of 28(a). For such superiors, Article 28(b)(i) requires that the superior 'knew, or consciously disregarded information which clearly indicated' the crimes. The argument relies on the lower threshold of 'should have known' from 28(a), which does not apply to the legal characterization of a civilian superior's liability under 28(b).

The question, however, is governed by Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute, which applies a single 'had reason to know' standard to all superiors, as does customary Rule 153. Moreover, the officer served as supreme ABiH commander, Chief of the Main Staff, and rotating Deputy Commander — military command positions — making the Article 28(a) standard applicable in any event.

objections.ground: The argument misstates the legal standard for 'punishment' in command responsibility by ignoring the specific requirement to 'submit the matter to competent authorities' as an alternative to direct punishment.
objections.reasoning: Article 28(b)(iii) and 28(a)(ii) require measures to 'prevent or repress their commission or to submit the matter to the competent authorities for investigation and prosecution.' The facts state the officer instructed cooperation with an investigation already underway by the 6th Corps Security Service. The argument fails to address whether this constituted a failure to 'submit the matter to competent authorities,' which is a valid discharge of the duty under the Statute, rather than asserting a requirement for direct punishment which is not the only legal standard.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The argument asserts a failure to punish by not ordering arrests or disciplinary action, but it ignores the explicit alternative in Article 28(a)(ii) and 28(b)(iii) of the Rome Statute and the corresponding duty under Article 7(3) to 'submit the matter to the competent authorities.' The facts state that an investigation was already underway by the 6th Corps Security Service and military police, and the officer instructed his team to cooperate with it. This constitutes submission to competent authorities, a legally sufficient measure.

objections.reasoning: The officer’s role was limited to consulting the commander and issuing orders only within his authority; the record does not show he had direct command of the 9th Brigade or the troops that committed the killings.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The facts do not establish that the officer exercised effective authority and control over the 9th Motorised Brigade or the specific troops that committed the murders. The officer's Inspection Team role was limited to coordination, monitoring, and consulting the Commander on drastic proposals, with order-issuing power only within his authority.

objections.reasoning: He learned of the killings only on the evening of 9 September, after the last proven killing, and there is no evidence that he had prior knowledge or that the circumstances required him to be aware.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The facts explicitly state that the officer learned of the crimes on the evening of 9 September, after the last proven killing. There is no evidence that he had prior knowledge or that the circumstances (coordinating role, billeting) gave him reason to know during the commission of the murders on 8–9 September. For the duty to prevent, knowledge must exist before or during the crimes; for the duty to punish, knowledge arose only after the fact.

objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection correctly notes that customary Rule 152 addresses liability for crimes committed pursuant to orders, which is a direct mode of liability, not command responsibility for failure to act. The argument's reliance on Rule 152 is therefore misplaced. objections.ground: The argument conflates the 'knew or should have known' standard of Article 28(a) with the distinct 'consciously disregarded' standard required for non-military superiors under Article 28(b).
objections.reasoning: The officer is described as a civilian Chief of Staff/Deputy Commander, not a 'military commander or person effectively acting as a military commander' in the direct sense of 28(a). The argument relies on the lower threshold of 'should have known' from 28(a), which does not apply to the legal characterization of a civilian superior's liability under 28(b).
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection relies on the Rome Statute's distinction between Article 28(a) ('should have known') for military commanders and Article 28(b) ('consciously disregarded') for other superiors. objections.ground: The argument misstates the legal standard for 'punishment' in command responsibility by ignoring the specific requirement to 'submit the matter to competent authorities' as an alternative to direct punishment.

The facts state the officer instructed cooperation with an investigation already underway by the 6th Corps Security Service. objections.disposition_reasoning: The argument asserts a failure to punish by not ordering arrests or disciplinary action, but it ignores the explicit alternative in Article 28(a)(ii) and 28(b)(iii) of the Rome Statute and the corresponding duty under Article 7(3) to 'submit the matter to the competent authorities.' objections.reasoning: Article 28(a) applies only to military commanders and persons effectively acting as military commanders in the context of international armed conflict. The officer was a civilian Chief of Staff in a non-international conflict. The correct standard for non-military superiors is Article 28(b), which requires effective authority and control and that crimes be within the superior's effective responsibility. Citing 28(a) mischaracterizes the applicable legal test and ignores the jurisdictional and definitional limits of the cited article.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection mischaracterizes the officer as a 'civilian Chief of Staff' and asserts Article 28(a) applies only in international armed conflict. The officer held military command positions (supreme commander, Chief of Main Staff, Deputy Commander of the ABiH). Article 28(a) applies to 'a military commander or person effectively acting as a military commander' without limiting its scope to international armed conflict. More importantly, the governing law is Article 7(3) of the ICTY Statute, which does not distinguish between military and civilian superiors for the knowledge standard.
